content: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is a large molecule composed of a lipid and a polysaccharide (carbohydrate) linked together by a covalent bond. Functions LPS is a critical component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. It plays a significant role in maintaining the structural integrity of the bacterial cell and protects the membrane from certain types of chemical attacks. LPS is classified as an endotoxin and elicits a strong immune response in normal animal immune systems. Among Gram-positive bacteria, only Listeria monocytogenes, a common pathogen found in unpasteurized milk, possesses LPS. LPS serves as the prototypical endotoxin because it binds to the CD14/TLR4/MD2 receptor complex. This interaction triggers the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines in various cell types, particularly macrophages. In immunology, an LPS challenge refers to exposing a subject to LPS, which can act as a toxin. LPS also increases the negative charge of the bacterial cell membrane and contributes to the stabilization of the overall membrane structure. The lipid portion of LPS, such as hydroxymyristic acid, is embedded in the outer membrane, while the rest of the LPS molecule extends outward from the bacterial surface. This structural arrangement is a key factor in its toxicity. The core oligosaccharide of LPS is attached to lipid A, which is partially responsible for the toxic effects of Gram-negative bacteria. O-antigen The polysaccharide side chain of LPS is referred to as the O-antigen. This O side chain is a polysaccharide chain that extends from the core polysaccharide. The composition of the O side chain varies among different strains of Gram-negative bacteria. The presence or absence of O chains determines whether the LPS is classified as rough or smooth. Full-length O chains result in smooth LPS, while the absence or reduction of O chains leads to rough LPS. Bacteria with rough LPS typically have more permeable cell membranes to hydrophobic antibiotics because rough LPS is more hydrophobic. O side chains are easily recognized by host antibodies; however, Gram-negative bacteria can modify the structure of these chains to evade immune detection. The structure of the core and O-antigen is often determined using techniques such as methylation analysis or NMR spectroscopy. LPS Modifications The biosynthesis of LPS can be modified to present specific sugar structures. These modifications can be recognized by other LPS molecules, which may inhibit LPS toxins, or by glycosyltransferases, which use these sugar structures to add additional specific sugars. Variability and Specificity The O-antigens, which are the outer carbohydrate components of LPS, are the most variable portion of the molecule and are responsible for its antigenic specificity. In contrast, lipid A is the most conserved part of the molecule, even across different bacterial genera. Variations in the number and nature of acyl chains in lipid A can influence its biological activity. Some of these variations may confer antagonistic properties to LPS. For example, Rhodobacter sphaeroides diphosphoryl lipid A (RsDPLA) acts as a potent antagonist of LPS in human cells but functions as an agonist in hamster and equine cells. It has been hypothesized that conical lipid A structures, such as those from E. coli, are more agonistic, while less conical lipid A structures, like those from Porphyromonas gingivalis, may activate different signaling pathways (e.g., TLR2 instead of TLR4). Completely cylindrical lipid A structures, such as those from Rhodobacter sphaeroides, are antagonistic to TLRs. Experimental Research The function of LPS has been extensively studied due to its role in activating numerous transcription factors. LPS also induces the production of various mediators involved in septic shock. Diversity The gene clusters responsible for LPS biosynthesis are highly variable among different strains, subspecies, and species of bacterial pathogens that infect plants and animals.
